terms.definition: A rule assigning a probability to every range of values a measurement could take, describing the population a reading is drawn from rather than the readings in hand. For a measurement that can take any value in a range it is drawn as a curve, and probability is read as the area under that curve between two values.

alignment.note: PREM-STA-002 uses distribution for the observed shape of a set of measured values, read off a histogram of the data you have. A probability distribution is the idealised object standing behind those values: it covers readings nobody recorded, extends past both ends of the data, and assigns probability rather than counts. The lesson draws the second over the first and then checks whether the fit holds.

terms.definition: A named probability distribution adopted to represent how one measurement is spread across its possible values, together with the parameter values chosen for it. Adopting one is a decision that can be checked against data and rejected, and this lesson treats the normal curve fitted to cohort fasting glucose as exactly that.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-010 defines a scientific model broadly as a selective representation of a system built to answer a stated question. This lesson narrows the word to one job: representing the spread of a single measurement across its possible values. It keeps the earlier lesson's discipline of stated assumptions, a domain of use, and tests that can fail, and it drops any claim about mechanism.

terms.definition: One specific continuous probability distribution: symmetric about its centre, single-humped, and fixed entirely by a mean and a standard deviation. The name collides with two other senses a reader already holds. In plain English normal means usual; in a clinic a normal result is one inside a laboratory reference range. Neither is implied here, and a measurement can follow a normal distribution while every value in it is clinically alarming.

A quantity that has to be supplied before a named distribution describes anything in particular. A normal distribution takes two: a location parameter, its mean, which places the centre, and a scale parameter, its standard deviation, which sets the spread. A binomial takes the number of trials and the probability of a yes result on one trial.

alignment.note: PREM-SCI-010 defines a model parameter as a model quantity held fixed during one run and free to change between runs. This lesson narrows the word to the quantities that identify one member of a distribution family, so that changing a parameter changes which curve you are using rather than which scenario you are running.

terms.definition: The height of a continuous distribution's curve at a given value. Density is not probability: probability is area under the curve between two values, so the probability that a continuous measurement takes any one exact value is zero, and a question about a continuous measurement has to name a range before it has an answer.

The statement that a normal distribution places 68.27 per cent of its values within one standard deviation of the mean, 95.45 per cent within two and 99.73 per cent within three, usually quoted as about 68, 95 and 99.7 per cent. These are exact areas of a mathematical curve, so they belong to the model and transfer to a dataset only to the extent that a normal distribution describes it.

A measurement re-expressed as its distance from the mean of a stated reference distribution, counted in standard deviations: z = (x − μ)/σ. It carries no units, so it compares quantities that share none, and it is unchanged by converting the original measurement between units. It reports distance only; turning it into a probability requires a distributional assumption that has been checked.

The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, which is what any normal measurement becomes once it has been standardised. Because every normal distribution maps onto this one, the same three percentages describe the bands at ±1, ±2 and ±3 for every measurement ever standardised.

A distribution whose values crowd towards the low end and thin out slowly towards the high end, so its mean sits above its median. Measurements with a floor and no ceiling tend to take this shape, fasting glucose and hospital length of stay among them, and no normal distribution can reproduce it because the normal family has no parameter that permits a lean.

A probability distribution over outcomes that can be listed one by one, such as the whole numbers 0 through 60. Unlike a continuous distribution it gives each individual outcome a probability of its own, so asking for the probability of exactly 49 has a real answer rather than zero.

The discrete distribution of the number of yes results in a fixed number of trials, when each trial has exactly two mutually exclusive outcomes, the probability of yes is the same on every trial, and the trials are independent. With n trials and probability p it puts the count's mean at np and its standard deviation at the square root of np(1 − p).
